narrativeReportMd:
# Claim R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
Breaking changes were found for local Claim content. The highest-impact forward migration issues are the mandatory `patient`→`subject` rename, the `item.bodySite` datatype/content-model replacement, and removed or moved nested elements such as `diagnosis.packageCode`, `careTeam.responsible`, and `careTeam.qualification`.

## Scope
The analysis used the local R4 and R6 core StructureDefinitions plus selected local ValueSet/CodeSystem files. It excludes inherited base-resource and datatype changes, Claim search parameters, operations, profiles, and jurisdiction-specific payer rules.

## Main migration themes
R6 generalizes several Claim concepts: recipients become `subject` and may be groups, body sites become repeatable CodeableReference-backed structures, supporting-info values become broadly typed, and multiple references accept new target resources. R6 also relaxes some R4 required fields, which helps forward validation but creates R6-to-R4 conversion gaps.

## Highest-impact findings
`Claim.patient` must be renamed to `Claim.subject` for every migrated instance. `Claim.item.bodySite` must be restructured rather than simply renamed. `Claim.supportingInfo.timingDate` must become `timingDateTime` or another R6 choice. DRG/package codes and care-team responsibility/qualification data require business-aware mapping.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important for body-site grouping, diagnosis-related-group migration when multiple diagnosis-level package codes exist, care-team responsibility/qualification semantics, line-item range semantics, and terminology preferences.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Most hard breaks could have been softened by retaining deprecated aliases or old choice types for one transition release. Several other changes are additive or looser and are forward-compatible but need profiles or conversion rules for systems that must emit R4.

## Follow-up analysis
Separate base-artifact reports should cover inherited DomainResource/Resource behavior. Datatype reports should cover CodeableReference and any broad `value[x]` datatype changes. Terminology review would improve confidence for preferred/example value set impacts.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: Claim has high-impact local breaking changes. Top concerns are the mandatory `patient`→`subject` rename, the `item.bodySite` content-model replacement, and removed/moved care-team and diagnosis billing elements. The main uncertainty is semantic intent without official change notes or narrative pages.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Forward migration requires element renames, choice-suffix changes, and structural rewrites. Reverse conversion from R6 to R4 is limited by widened reference targets, optionalized R4-required fields, new product/service range fields, Group subjects, multiple/referenced body sites, and the broad supporting-info value choice set.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural changes because both primary StructureDefinitions were present and directly compared. Confidence is medium for intent, prevalence, and terminology consequences because official diffs, narrative change notes, and full terminology expansions were not available locally.

findings.title: Mandatory Claim.patient was replaced by mandatory Claim.subject and the subject target widened

semanticText.short: The recipient of the products and services

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 serializes the required recipient as the JSON member `patient`.

semanticText.short: The recipient(s) of the products and services

newState.narrativeMd: R6 serializes the required recipient as `subject` and permits either a Patient or a Group.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements share role, cardinality, summary flag, and near-identical recipient definitions; R6 changes the name and widens targets.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct instance-shape break for every R4 Claim: the required R4 JSON member is `patient`, while R6 requires `subject`. A strict R6 validator will reject untransformed R4 instances for the old member and missing `subject`. R6 `Group` subjects cannot be represented as R4 `Claim.patient` without policy-specific handling.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The recipient is central to billing and adjudication; incorrect migration can associate a claim with the wrong patient or group.

justification.inferredGoal: Generalize the recipient from a patient-only element to the common `subject` pattern and support group claims.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `patient` with Patient or Group targets and clearer recipient wording, or accept it as a deprecated alias during transition.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Generalizing the claim recipient to include groups is reasonable, but renaming a required element breaks essentially every untransformed R4 Claim. The same patient-or-group recipient goal could mostly be met without changing the base member name, and the local evidence does not show that the `subject` rename was necessary.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: `Claim.patient` could have been retained as the base recipient element, target-widened to Patient or Group, and documented as the Claim subject. If `subject` was added as the preferred name, the old path could be a deprecated alias with a consistency rule; the cost is lingering duplicate recipient fields and a less tidy model.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Keeps a nonoptimal `patient` name for Group claims; aliasing would add duplicate recipient representations.

evidence.detail: R4 defines required `Claim.patient` with target Patient.
R6 defines required `Claim.subject` with target Patient or Group.

examples.examplesMd: Fragments are illustrative. Patient references map by renaming; Group subjects require a local R4 policy.

findings.narrativeMd: `Claim.patient` is absent from R6 and the corresponding recipient element is `Claim.subject`. Because FHIR JSON member names are element names, this is a serialized data break as well as a generated-code property rename.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 Claim with `patient` and no `subject` is old-valid/new-invalid. A Patient subject maps back to R4, but a Group subject is not cleanly R4-representable.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `Claim.patient` to `Claim.subject`, update FHIRPath/search/index code, and add tests for Patient and Group subjects. For R6 Group subjects, use an extension, reject reverse conversion, or split claims according to local policy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change likely aligns Claim with common FHIR `subject` conventions. A deprecated alias would have been less disruptive but would require consistency rules between two recipient elements.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 requires `Claim.patient` as `Reference(Patient)`, while R6 removes that member and requires `Claim.subject` as `Reference(Patient|Group)`. An untransformed R4 Claim is therefore missing the required R6 element and has an unknown old member, and generated models/FHIRPath expressions also move from `patient` to `subject`. The R6 goal of supporting group subjects is reasonable, but this is a required, central billing-recipient path and a less disruptive base design appears available.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `Claim.patient` min=1 max=1 type `Reference(Patient)`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `Claim.subject` min=1 max=1 type `Reference(Patient|Group)`; no R6 `Claim.patient` element.
R4 maturity map: Claim is FMM 2, trial-use.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral: it does not create normative stability pressure, but it also does not soften this required-path, high-use billing-recipient break.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 instances with required `patient` and no `subject` fail R6 structure validation; runtime/API/codegen also changes the property name, and R6 `Group` subjects introduce R6-to-R4 loss.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have retained `Claim.patient` as the recipient element and widened its target to Patient or Group, or kept `patient` as a deprecated alias while introducing `subject`. The tradeoff is an imperfect name for Group claims or duplicate recipient fields requiring consistency rules, but the base break for every R4 Claim would be avoided.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing High impact and Yes alternative judgment; the independent assessment also finds the rename disproportionate enough to revisit.

findings.title: Claim.supportingInfo.timing[x] removed the R4 `date` choice and added `dateTime`/`Timing`

oldState.narrativeMd: A simple date is serialized as `timingDate`.

newState.summary: R6 permits `timingDateTime`, `timingPeriod`, or `timingTiming`; `timingDate` is no longer valid.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 replaces the date choice with dateTime and adds Timing.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using `supportingInfo.timingDate` are invalid in R6 because the choice suffix changed. R6 `Timing` values have no R4 choice equivalent.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow timestamps and scheduled/repeating timing for supporting information.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the `date` choice while adding `dateTime` and `Timing`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding `dateTime` and `Timing` is a reasonable expressiveness goal. Dropping the existing `date` choice creates a serialized-name break for `timingDate`, and the local definitions do not show why retaining `date` would have prevented the R6 goal.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have allowed `timingDate`, `timingDateTime`, `timingPeriod`, and `timingTiming`. That would preserve all R4 timing-date instances while still allowing timestamps and repeating schedules. The main cost is a longer choice list and possible duplicate date-only encodings that implementations would need to normalize.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Adds an extra choice suffix and duplicate date-only representations, but preserves R4 instances.

evidence.detail: R4 choice types are `date` and `Period`.
R6 choice types are `dateTime`, `Period`, and `Timing`.

examples.examplesMd: A date-only value can often be copied to `timingDateTime`, but the member name must change.

findings.narrativeMd: The choice-type set changed locally. The old `date` choice was removed, so `timingDate` is no longer an R6 member; `Timing` creates new R6 content that R4 cannot express.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `timingPeriod` remains compatible, but R4 `timingDate` is old-valid/new-invalid. R6 `timingTiming` is not R4-representable; R6 `dateTime` can down-convert only when loss of time/timezone detail is acceptable.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Transform `timingDate` to `timingDateTime` and preserve precision. For reverse conversion, reject or extension-map `Timing`; down-convert `dateTime` only under explicit business rules.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding expressive choices was likely justified. Removing `date` was probably avoidable by retaining it for a transition period.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 allowed `supportingInfo.timingDate` and `timingPeriod`; R6 allows `timingDateTime`, `timingPeriod`, and `timingTiming`. The added `dateTime` and `Timing` choices are useful, but removing the existing `date` choice changes the serialized choice suffix for date-only supporting information. A date-only R4 value can usually be represented semantically as a date-precision `dateTime`, but the wire member and generated choice accessor still break.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `Claim.supportingInfo.timing[x]` types are `date` and `Period`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `Claim.supportingInfo.timing[x]` types are `dateTime`, `Period`, and `Timing`.
The path is optional supporting information, not a whole-resource behavior change.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. Because the affected path is optional, FMM does not by itself make the change high-impact, but the avoidable choice-suffix break still matters.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: an R4 `timingDate` member is not an R6 choice member; R6 `Timing` also creates R6-to-R4 loss, and `dateTime` reverse conversion can be lossy when time or timezone detail is present.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have retained `date` while adding `dateTime` and `Timing`. That would preserve R4 instances and still meet the expressiveness goal; the cost is a longer choice list and duplicate date-only encodings that receivers may normalize.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing Medium hard-break assessment and Yes alternative judgment; the fresh review emphasizes that retaining `date` is a modest base-design cost.

findings.title: Claim.item.bodySite changed from CodeableConcept to a repeating backbone with CodeableReference site entries

oldState.summary: R4 has `item.bodySite` as `CodeableConcept` 0..1 and `item.subSite` as a sibling repeating CodeableConcept.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 represents the primary body site directly and sub-sites as sibling values.

newState.summary: R6 has `item.bodySite` as `BackboneElement` 0..* with required repeating `site` CodeableReference(BodyStructure) and optional nested `subSite`.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 nests coded or referenced sites and sub-sites inside a repeating bodySite component.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The retained path name masks a content-model replacement; the old `subSite` sibling is now nested under the new backbone.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4 CodeableConcept at `item.bodySite` is not a valid R6 BackboneElement, and R4 `item.subSite` no longer exists. Generated types and FHIRPath expressions change substantially. R6 can express multiple body sites and BodyStructure references that R4 cannot carry losslessly.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Body-site and tooth-surface data can directly affect dental, accident, and procedure adjudication.

justification.inferredGoal: Support multiple body sites and coded or referenced BodyStructure locations with associated sub-sites.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add a new detailed repeating body-site element while retaining old `bodySite` and `subSite` during transition.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of representing multiple body sites, BodyStructure references, and nested sub-sites is reasonable. A less-breaking transitional design exists, but it would leave two same-resource ways to describe the anatomy and would be especially ambiguous when multiple sites and old sibling sub-sites are both present.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have kept the R4 `item.bodySite` CodeableConcept and sibling `item.subSite`, then added a new optional backbone such as `bodySiteDetail` for repeatable CodeableReference sites with nested sub-sites. This would preserve R4 instances, but deprecated anatomy fields could persist indefinitely and systems would need precedence and consistency rules when both representations appear.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids an immediate hard break but duplicates anatomy semantics and leaves ambiguous site/sub-site association rules.

evidence.detail: R4 `item.bodySite` is 0..1 CodeableConcept.
R4 `item.subSite` is a repeating CodeableConcept sibling.
R6 `item.bodySite` is a repeating BackboneElement.
R6 requires at least one `site` CodeableReference for each bodySite component.

examples.examplesMd: The old CodeableConcept maps to `bodySite[0].site[0].concept`; old `subSite` values move under the same bodySite entry.

findings.narrativeMd: `Claim.item.bodySite` is a same-name path with a different datatype and nested content. This is a high-risk serialization and code-generation break.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 line items with `bodySite` or `subSite` need restructuring for R6. R6 line items with multiple sites or BodyStructure references cannot be represented losslessly in R4.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Create an R6 `bodySite` array when old `bodySite` or `subSite` exists. Map the old CodeableConcept to `bodySite[0].site[0].concept` and old sub-sites to `bodySite[0].subSite`. For R6-to-R4, only single coded sites map cleanly.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The more expressive model is useful, but replacing an existing datatype at the same path was probably avoidable through a new optional element or transitional alias.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `Claim.item.bodySite` is a single `CodeableConcept` with repeating sibling `item.subSite`; R6 turns `item.bodySite` into a repeating backbone whose required `site` entries are `CodeableReference(BodyStructure)` and whose `subSite` values are nested. This is a real structure and generated-type break for item anatomy, and R6 can represent multiple sites or BodyStructure references that R4 cannot. However, the R6 model directly improves site/sub-site association and reference support, and the obvious less-breaking design would leave two competing anatomy representations in the same resource.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `Claim.item.bodySite` max=1 type `CodeableConcept`; `Claim.item.subSite` max=* type `CodeableConcept`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `Claim.item.bodySite` max=* type `BackboneElement`; `Claim.item.bodySite.site` min=1 max=* type `CodeableReference(BodyStructure)`.
R6 nests `Claim.item.bodySite.subSite` under each body-site component.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. The body-site path is billing-relevant, but the resource is not mature enough for that alone to outweigh a well-motivated content-model improvement.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: an R4 `bodySite` CodeableConcept is not an R6 backbone element and R4 `item.subSite` is absent; runtime/API/codegen types change, with R6-to-R4 loss for multiple sites or BodyStructure references.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. R6 could have kept the old `bodySite`/`subSite` fields and added a new detailed repeating anatomy element, but that would create duplicate same-resource representations and hard precedence/consistency rules when both old and new anatomy fields are populated.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing High impact and Partial alternative judgment; the break is substantial, but the fresh assessment treats the R6 model goal and the alternative's ambiguity as sufficient to make it probably OK.

findings.title: Claim.diagnosis.packageCode moved to root Claim.diagnosisRelatedGroup

oldState.summary: R4 has optional `Claim.diagnosis.packageCode` inside each diagnosis component.
oldState.narrativeMd: The package/DRG code was associated with a diagnosis repetition.

newState.summary: R6 removes the nested element and adds optional root `Claim.diagnosisRelatedGroup`.
newState.narrativeMd: The code is now a single claim-level value.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements share short label, definition, comment, and value set; the path/context changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances with `diagnosis.packageCode` fail R6 validation. A single distinct code can be moved to the root, but multiple diagnosis-level package codes cannot be mapped losslessly to the single R6 root element.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: DRG/package codes can materially affect reimbursement grouping.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent diagnosis-related group as a claim-level billing grouping.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep deprecated `diagnosis.packageCode` alongside root `diagnosisRelatedGroup`, or provide a repeatable association preserving diagnosis context.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Representing the diagnosis-related group as a claim-level billing grouping is reasonable and matches the R6 root element. Retaining the old nested field would soften migration, but it would also preserve a per-diagnosis representation for a concept that appears intended to be claim-level and would require conflict rules for multiple nested codes.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking design could have retained `Claim.diagnosis.packageCode` as deprecated while adding `Claim.diagnosisRelatedGroup`. That preserves R4 instances and single-code migrations, but if both root and nested values appear, or if multiple diagnoses have different package codes, validators and receivers need nontrivial consistency and precedence rules.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old per-diagnosis data but conflicts with claim-level DRG semantics and risks inconsistent or multiple codes.

evidence.detail: R4 defines package billing code under each diagnosis.
R6 defines the same package billing/DRG text at Claim root.

examples.examplesMd: The transform is clean only when at most one distinct package code is present.

findings.narrativeMd: The package billing/DRG code moved from a diagnosis child to the Claim root. That is both a path break and a semantic context change.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 data using `diagnosis.packageCode` is old-valid/new-invalid. R6 root `diagnosisRelatedGroup` can be down-converted only if local rules identify which R4 diagnosis should carry it.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Detect all old package codes. If exactly one distinct code exists, map it to `diagnosisRelatedGroup`; if multiple exist, use extensions or manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The move was likely motivated by claim-level DRG semantics, but a deprecated nested alias would have reduced migration ambiguity.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 stores the package billing or DRG code under each diagnosis as `Claim.diagnosis.packageCode`; R6 removes that child and introduces a single root `Claim.diagnosisRelatedGroup`. This is more than a path move because the context changes from per-diagnosis to per-claim. Single-code migrations are straightforward, but multiple diagnosis-level package codes cannot be carried losslessly into one root element, and DRG/package codes are directly reimbursement-relevant.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `Claim.diagnosis.packageCode` max=1 type `CodeableConcept`, definition covers package billing or DRG code.
R6 StructureDefinition: `Claim.diagnosisRelatedGroup` max=1 type `CodeableConcept` with the same package billing/DRG definition at Claim root.
R4 packageCode requirements refer to relating the current diagnosis to a package billing code.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral, so the judgment is driven by the path-level lossiness and reimbursement relevance rather than by a high maturity guarantee.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 `diagnosis.packageCode` is not an R6 element; R6-to-R4 loss and expert-dependent migration occur when multiple old diagnosis-level codes or a single R6 root code must be assigned back to a specific diagnosis.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. R6 could have retained a deprecated diagnosis-level package code while adding the root DRG, or added a repeatable association that preserves diagnosis context. The tradeoff is real conflict and precedence handling between per-diagnosis and claim-level DRG semantics, but the current single root field loses distinctions R4 could express.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing Medium impact and Partial alternative judgment; the fresh review gives more weight to lossy, business-critical migration and therefore marks this for revisit.

findings.title: Claim.careTeam.responsible was removed without a direct R6 replacement

oldState.summary: R4 has optional boolean `Claim.careTeam.responsible` for the lead/responsible practitioner.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could mark one care team member as billing and/or responsible.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 retains sequence, provider, role, and specialty but not the boolean responsible marker.

facts.note: No direct replacement was found in R6 Claim.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 careTeam entries containing `responsible` are invalid in R6. The information can affect billing responsibility and lead-practitioner logic, and R6 provides no computable boolean equivalent.

justification.inferredGoal: Possibly remove duplicate responsibility semantics in favor of provider or role-based representation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the optional `responsible` boolean as deprecated, or define a normative coded role equivalent.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The local R6 definitions remove the element without a direct replacement or stated rationale. If the goal was to avoid duplicate responsibility semantics, retaining the optional boolean as deprecated or tying it to a coded role would preserve existing data with modest long-term cost.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have kept `Claim.careTeam.responsible` as an optional deprecated boolean and clarified how it relates to `careTeam.role` or the root provider. That would preserve R4-valid instances and avoid silent loss of lead-practitioner information; the tradeoff is one additional legacy flag that overlaps with richer role coding.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Some overlap with role/provider semantics, but low base-model cost for preserving a simple R4 flag.

evidence.detail: R4 defines the optional boolean responsible indicator.
R6 careTeam child list contains no `responsible` element.

examples.examplesMd: A possible migration is to encode responsibility in `careTeam.role`, but the base definitions do not prescribe a code.

findings.narrativeMd: The R4 boolean identifying the lead or responsible care team member disappeared from R6. This is a hard validation break and possible semantic loss.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `careTeam.responsible` are old-valid/new-invalid. Reverse conversion is structurally simpler because there is no R6 counterpart, but migrated R4 information must not be silently dropped.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory use of `careTeam.responsible` and define a mapping to `careTeam.role`, an extension, or a documented business rule. Test multiple-care-team-member cases.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The removal was avoidable by retaining the optional boolean as deprecated. Without rationale, implementations may choose inconsistent replacements.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 had an optional `Claim.careTeam.responsible` boolean identifying the billing or responsible party and distinguishing the lead member when multiple parties are present. R6 keeps `careTeam` and `role` but has no direct boolean replacement. R4 instances using the flag fail R6 validation, and automated migration risks losing lead-responsibility semantics unless a local coded-role or extension policy is chosen.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `Claim.careTeam.responsible` min=0 max=1 type `boolean`.
R4 requirements: when multiple parties are present it is required to distinguish the lead or responsible individual.
R6 StructureDefinition careTeam children include no `responsible` element.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral, but the path carries billing responsibility semantics and the element was a small optional flag, so the maturity context does not justify silent removal.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 careTeam entries containing `responsible` are invalid in R6; runtime/API/codegen loses the boolean and migration can become semantic/documentation-dependent.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have kept the optional boolean as deprecated, or defined a clear coded-role equivalent and transition rule. Keeping one legacy boolean has modest base-model cost compared with the risk of inconsistent local mappings.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing Medium impact and Yes alternative judgment; the independent review also finds the removal avoidable enough to revisit.

findings.title: Claim.careTeam.qualification was replaced by narrower Claim.careTeam.specialty semantics

oldState.summary: R4 `qualification` allowed practitioner credential or specialization.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 text covered both credentials and specializations.

newState.summary: R6 `specialty` is optional CodeableConcept for practitioner/provider specialization.
newState.narrativeMd: The new name and definition narrow the concept to specialization.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The elements share datatype, cardinality, and value set, but textual semantics narrowed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The old path is removed, so R4 instances with `careTeam.qualification` need transformation. Specialty values can likely map; credential/license values may not satisfy the narrower R6 semantics.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that the relevant care-team attribute is service specialty rather than general credential.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add `specialty` while retaining `qualification` for credentials or as a deprecated broad legacy field.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Clarifying that the R6 field is a specialization is reasonable, but the R4 field also covered credentials. The local evidence does not show why credential-capable `qualification` had to be removed or renamed rather than retained with clearer semantics.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking design could have introduced `careTeam.specialty` for specializations while keeping `careTeam.qualification` for credentials or legacy values. This would preserve R4 instances and avoid forcing credential values into a narrower specialty field, but implementations would need rules for old qualification values that are really specialties and for cases where both fields are populated.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves broad R4 values but creates overlapping qualification/specialty representations and validation ambiguity.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `qualification` as practitioner credential or specialization.
R6 defines `specialty` as practitioner/provider specialization.

examples.examplesMd: The example is safe only when the old value is truly a specialty rather than a credential.

findings.narrativeMd: `Claim.careTeam.qualification` appears to become `Claim.careTeam.specialty`, but the meaning narrows from credential-or-specialization to specialization.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Any R4 use of `careTeam.qualification` is old-valid/new-invalid. A direct rename preserves syntax but can change meaning if the value was a credential.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map clear specialty values to `careTeam.specialty`; preserve credentials in extensions or provider records. Review local value sets before automated rename.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A transition retaining `qualification` would have been less disruptive. The chosen rename improves clarity but requires human review for mixed credential/specialty code systems.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `Claim.careTeam.qualification` covered a practitioner credential or specialization; R6 uses `Claim.careTeam.specialty` for practitioner or provider specialization. Although the datatype and value set are similar, the name and semantics narrow. R4 credential values are old-valid/new-invalid at the wire level and may not be safely mapped to a specialty without terminology or business review.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `Claim.careTeam.qualification` max=1 type `CodeableConcept`, short text `Practitioner credential or specialization`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `Claim.careTeam.specialty` max=1 type `CodeableConcept`, definition says specialization applicable for the service.
Both elements use the provider-qualification value set, but the R6 field name and prose focus on specialty.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. The trial-use status allows model clarification, but it does not remove the concern that credential data may be forced into a narrower specialty field.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid plus semantic/documentation: R4 `careTeam.qualification` is absent in R6, and some old values lose meaning if mechanically renamed to `specialty`.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. R6 could have added `specialty` while retaining `qualification` for credentials or legacy values. That avoids invalidating R4 data, but it creates overlapping fields and requires rules for values that are both qualifications and specialties.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing Medium impact and Partial alternative judgment; the fresh review agrees the evidence is not clearly justified and treats the semantic narrowing as revisit-worthy.

findings.title: Provider, priority, and insurance requirements were relaxed, creating R6-to-R4 gaps

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 validators and generated models commonly assume these root elements are present.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 accepts Claims that omit these fields.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is forward-compatible but R6-valid claims can omit fields that R4 required. R4-era business logic may also encounter null/absent values where it assumed non-null.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow more flexible Claim use cases such as drafts, self-pay, or details supplied elsewhere.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed because the change loosens cardinality.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Lowering minimum cardinalities for `provider`, `priority`, and `insurance` does not invalidate R4 instances. It weakens base guarantees and creates reverse-conversion gaps, but as an R4-to-R6 compatibility question this is not a breaking base-design issue.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: For exchanges that need R4-like guarantees, R6 profiles can require these elements and converters can reject or default missing values. Those are policy and conversion controls rather than backward-compatible base-design alternatives, because the base R6 change already preserves R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Forward-compatible flexibility shifts burden to profiles and R6-to-R4 converters for missing data.

evidence.detail: R4 `provider` min is 1.
R6 `provider` min is 0.
R4 `priority` min is 1.
R6 `priority` min is 0.
R4 `insurance` min is 1.
R6 `insurance` min is 0.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment omits fields that R4 required; an R6 profile may still require them.

findings.narrativeMd: Several root-level requirements were relaxed. Existing R4 instances remain valid with respect to these fields, but reverse conversion and nullability assumptions change.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R6-to-R4 conversion must add, derive, reject, or extension-map missing provider, priority, and insurance. Runtime code should treat these R6 properties as optional.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Define defaulting/rejection/profile rules for missing fields and test each omission independently.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This is a loosening, so no forward compatibility alternative is needed. The burden shifts to profiles and converters.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 lowers the minimum cardinality of `Claim.provider`, `Claim.priority`, and `Claim.insurance` from required to optional. That weakens base guarantees and creates reverse-conversion or nullability work for systems processing R6 Claims, but it does not invalidate any R4 Claim. For exchanges that still require these fields, an R6 profile can restore the R4-like requirements without needing a different base design.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `Claim.provider`, `Claim.priority`, and `Claim.insurance` have min=1.
R6 StructureDefinition: the same paths have min=0.
Definitions and requirements for priority and insurance remain substantially similar while cardinality is loosened.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. Because this is a loosening with no old-valid/new-invalid effect, the maturity status does not push the finding toward revisit.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R6 instances may omit fields that R4 required, and generated R6 models expose optional properties; there is no R4-to-R6 instance break.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable for R4-to-R6 compatibility. Keeping the fields required would preserve stronger base guarantees but would reduce R6 flexibility; profiles are the appropriate mechanism for workflows that need R4-style completeness.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree with the existing Medium impact framing; agree that no less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed, but the fresh review treats this reverse-only issue as no problem.

findings.title: Line-item productOrService became optional and productOrServiceEnd added range semantics

oldState.summary: R4 requires productOrService 1..1 at item, detail, and subDetail levels; no range-end element exists.
oldState.narrativeMd: Every populated R4 line/detail/subdetail had a required billing or service code.

newState.summary: R6 makes productOrService 0..1 at all three levels and adds optional productOrServiceEnd at all three levels.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 supports code ranges and no longer requires the starting code in base cardinality.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 coded lines remain valid in R6, but R6 data may omit codes that R4 requires or use `productOrServiceEnd`, which R4 has no field for. Code assuming every line has a code must change.

justification.inferredGoal: Support ranges of product/service codes and more flexible grouping/preauthorization scenarios.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 compatibility alternative is needed because existing `productOrService` values remain valid.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding `productOrServiceEnd` and loosening `productOrService` minimum cardinality preserves existing R4 coded line items while enabling code-range scenarios. The compatibility cost is primarily for R6-to-R4 conversion and for R6 processors that must handle omitted or range-based line coding.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 profiles can re-require `productOrService` and restrict or ban `productOrServiceEnd` where exact R4-style line coding is required. That is not a backward-compatible base alternative for this finding because the R6 base change does not make R4 instances invalid.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Range flexibility and optional starts create R6-to-R4 conversion and adjudication-rule burden.

evidence.detail: R4 item productOrService min is 1.
R6 item productOrService min is 0 and definition mentions productOrServiceEnd ranges.
R6 adds item productOrServiceEnd.

examples.examplesMd: R4 cannot represent the range-end element and requires productOrService at each populated level.

findings.narrativeMd: The line-item code is no longer required in R6 and a range-end element was added at item/detail/subDetail levels.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 is safe for existing coded lines. R6-to-R4 must derive, reject, expand, or extension-map ranges and missing product/service codes.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update processing to handle absent productOrService and productOrServiceEnd; define reverse-conversion rules for code ranges.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The range feature required a new element, but base cardinality loosening means profiles should enforce exact line coding where adjudication requires it.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 makes `productOrService` optional at item, detail, and subDetail levels and adds matching `productOrServiceEnd` fields for code ranges. Existing R4 coded line items remain valid in R6, so this is not a forward instance break. The compatibility burden is still real because product/service coding is central to claim adjudication, R6 processors must handle missing or range-based codes, and R6-to-R4 conversion may need rejection, expansion, or extensions.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `Claim.item.productOrService`, `Claim.item.detail.productOrService`, and `Claim.item.detail.subDetail.productOrService` have min=1.
R6 StructureDefinition: the same paths have min=0 and mention use with `productOrServiceEnd` ranges.
R6 adds `productOrServiceEnd` at item, detail, and subDetail levels.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. The affected path is billing-central, so the reverse/nullability burden is not dismissed, but trial-use status supports proportionate model evolution.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss and runtime/API/codegen: R6 line items can omit R4-required codes or use code ranges, and generated R6 models make a previously required billing code optional; R4-to-R6 instances with a code remain valid.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No R4-to-R6 alternative is required because R4 data is preserved. A stricter base could have kept `productOrService` required while adding `productOrServiceEnd`, but that may block R6 use cases with grouped, deferred, or lower-level coding; R6 profiles can re-require exact line codes where needed.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing Medium, reverse-direction impact and Not applicable alternative judgment; the fresh review classifies the burden as real but proportionate.

findings.title: Claim.supportingInfo.value[x] expanded from five choices to a broad Any-style datatype set

oldState.summary: R4 permits boolean, string, Quantity, Attachment, or Reference(Resource).

newState.summary: R6 permits a broad set of primitive, complex, metadata, and special-purpose datatypes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 values remain allowed, but R6 choice handling expands dramatically. Most new suffixes cannot be represented at the R4 path without lossy conversion, indirection, or extension.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow supporting information to carry the datatype that best matches the evidence.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 alternative is needed because the choice set was widened.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R4 choice types remain accepted in R6, so this is not a forward instance break. The broader choice set plausibly improves fidelity for supporting information, while the main downside is R6-to-R4 representability and implementation complexity.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Profiles can constrain the R6 choice set to the R4-compatible subset for bidirectional exchanges. A smaller base expansion would reduce code complexity but would also provide less structured support for R6 evidence values; it is not needed to preserve R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Better expressiveness increases generated-code branching and reverse-conversion complexity.

evidence.detail: R4 has five choice types.
R6 has a broad list of choice types.

examples.examplesMd: `valueMoney` is valid in R6 but has no native R4 choice at this path.

findings.narrativeMd: `Claim.supportingInfo.value[x]` was widened dramatically, improving expressiveness but changing generated choice handling and reverse conversion.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No R4-valid value is invalidated. R6 values using new choice suffixes are not cleanly R4-representable except by extension, indirection, or lossy transformation.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update choice-switching code to handle or reject new suffixes. Define per-category reverse mappings rather than converting all values to strings.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This is forward-compatible and likely intentional; a smaller choice expansion would be easier but less semantically rich.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 greatly expands `Claim.supportingInfo.value[x]`, but the R4 choices remain allowed. This is an additive/widening change: R4 values using boolean, string, Quantity, Attachment, or Reference are still structurally valid in R6. New R6 suffixes increase generated-code branching and may not convert back to R4, but that is an expected consequence of broader expressiveness rather than a reason to revisit the base model.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `supportingInfo.value[x]` types include boolean, string, Quantity, Attachment, and Reference(Resource).
R6 StructureDefinition: the same path includes those types plus a broad set of primitive, datatype, and metadata choices.
The path name and cardinality remain the same.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. Since the change is widening-only for R4 instances, FMM does not create a compatibility concern.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: new R6 choice suffixes often have no R4 equivalent; no old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 mechanism is present.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable for backward compatibility. R6 profiles can restrict the choice set for bidirectional R4 exchanges; limiting the base expansion would reduce implementation branching but also reduce useful evidence fidelity.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree with the existing Medium overall impact as a fresh R4-to-R6 concern; agree that no less-breaking base alternative is needed for preserving R4 instances.

findings.title: Several existing Claim references widened their allowed target resources

oldState.summary: R4 has narrower reference target sets for enterer, facility, prescription, and originalPrescription.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 limits enterer to Practitioner/PractitionerRole, facility to Location, and prescription references to DeviceRequest/MedicationRequest/VisionPrescription.

newState.summary: R6 adds Patient/RelatedPerson to enterer, Organization to facility, and ServiceRequest to prescription/originalPrescription.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 permits more actors and request types in existing reference elements.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Widened targets do not invalidate R4 data in R6. They do create R6-to-R4 validation risk and affect generated reference unions, authorization rules, and search/index logic.

justification.inferredGoal: Support more realistic entry actors, facilities represented as organizations, and ServiceRequest-based prescriptions/referrals.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking R4-to-R6 alternative is needed because reference targets were only widened.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding target resource types preserves all R4-valid references at these paths and is the normal forward-compatible way to broaden a reference. The material compatibility risk is reverse conversion when R6 uses a newly allowed target.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Bidirectional R4-compatible exchanges can constrain R6 profiles to the R4 target subset. That does not count as a less-breaking base R6 design here because target widening itself does not break R4-to-R6 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: New target resources improve modeling but require R6-to-R4 rejection, substitution, or extension rules.

evidence.detail: R4 enterer targets Practitioner and PractitionerRole.
R6 enterer also targets Patient and RelatedPerson.
R4 facility targets Location only.
R6 facility also targets Organization.
R6 prescription adds ServiceRequest; originalPrescription does likewise.

examples.examplesMd: Each shown target is allowed by R6 at that path but not by R4.

findings.narrativeMd: Several references retained their names but widened target profiles. This is easy to miss because common old target types still work.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 is safe. R6-to-R4 conversion must check targets and reject, substitute, or extension-map new target resources.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update generated unions, validators, access-control checks, and search indexes. For bidirectional exchange, constrain profiles to the R4 target subset or implement target-specific conversion.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This is additive and forward-compatible; reverse conversion limitations are inherent once new targets are allowed.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The affected references keep their existing paths and R4 target types while adding more target resource types in R6. Widening reference targets is forward-compatible for R4 instances. Implementers still need to update generated unions, authorization checks, and R6-to-R4 converters for the new targets, but that is normal additive model evolution and can be constrained by profiles for bidirectional exchange.
keyEvidence: R4 `Claim.enterer` targets Practitioner and PractitionerRole; R6 also allows Patient and RelatedPerson.
R4 `Claim.facility` targets Location; R6 also allows Organization.
R6 `Claim.prescription` and `Claim.originalPrescription` add ServiceRequest while retaining the R4 targets.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. Because target widening does not invalidate R4 references, maturity status does not increase the compatibility concern.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss and runtime/API/codegen: new target types need converter and union-type handling, but no R4-valid reference becomes invalid in R6.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable for R4-to-R6 compatibility. A narrower R6 base would avoid reverse-conversion checks but would also forgo the intended broader actor, facility, and order representations; profiles can constrain target sets where necessary.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing reverse-conversion concerns and Not applicable alternative judgment, but disagree with treating the widening as a meaningful R4-to-R6 problem.

findings.title: Several local example terminology bindings were strengthened to preferred

oldState.summary: R4 uses example bindings for priority, fundsReserve, careTeam.role, supportingInfo.category, diagnosis.type, diagnosis.onAdmission, and procedure.type.
oldState.narrativeMd: Example bindings do not express a preference for in-set codes.

newState.summary: R6 changes those bindings to preferred while retaining the same value set URLs.
newState.narrativeMd: Preferred bindings are not usually fatal, but they express a stronger interoperability expectation.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Preferred bindings generally do not make out-of-set CodeableConcepts invalid, unlike required bindings. The risk is terminology warnings, profile derivation, QA gates, and tooling that treats preferred bindings strongly.

justification.inferredGoal: Improve interoperability by recommending common value sets for adjudication codes.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking base alternative is needed because preferred bindings do not invalidate base instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Moving example bindings to preferred bindings is a reasonable interoperability signal and remains a weak conformance constraint in the base resource. Since out-of-set CodeableConcepts are not made invalid by a preferred binding, this is not a hard R4-to-R6 breaking design issue.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Keeping example bindings would reduce terminology warnings but would also provide weaker guidance. Implementations and profiles can still decide how strongly to enforce preferred value sets; no base-design alternative is needed to preserve R4 instance validity.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Stronger terminology guidance can produce warnings or QA burden but not required-code validation failure.

evidence.detail: R4 priority binding strength is example.
R6 priority binding strength is preferred.
R4 supportingInfo.category binding strength is example.
R6 supportingInfo.category binding strength is preferred.

examples.examplesMd: A locally coded `Claim.priority` remains structurally valid against the base resource, but R6 QA or derived profiles may apply stronger expectations.

findings.narrativeMd: A set of local coded elements moved from example to preferred bindings. This is not hard instance-breaking, but it changes conformance expectations.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Base R6 validation should still accept CodeableConcepts outside preferred value sets. The practical risk is behavioral and conformance-related.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review local code systems for the affected elements and prefer the referenced value sets where practical. Do not blindly map codes without terminology review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Preferred binding is a backward-compatible way to improve terminology alignment, though CI or certification tooling may treat warnings as failures.

freshReview.narrativeMd: Several Claim CodeableConcept bindings move from example to preferred. A preferred binding recommends a value set but does not make out-of-set codes structurally invalid in the base resource. The practical effect is terminology guidance and possible warnings or QA pressure, not a hard R4-to-R6 instance break.
keyEvidence: R4 `Claim.priority`, `fundsReserve`, `careTeam.role`, `supportingInfo.category`, `diagnosis.type`, `diagnosis.onAdmission`, and `procedure.type` bindings are example.
R6 changes those same bindings to preferred while keeping CodeableConcept datatypes.
FHIR binding strength preferred is weaker than required and does not by itself reject other CodeableConcept codings.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral. The change is warning-level terminology guidance, so FMM does not create a revisit concern.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: warning-level: preferred bindings may produce terminology warnings or stricter local QA behavior, but base R6 validation should still accept out-of-set CodeableConcepts.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable. Keeping example bindings would be less noisy but would weaken interoperability guidance; no base design change is needed to preserve R4 instance validity.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing Low impact and Not applicable alternative judgment.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds optional status, tracking, encounter/event, and patient-payment elements
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Optional additions such as `traceNumber`, `statusReason`, root `encounter`, `event`, `patientPaid`, and item/detail/subDetail `traceNumber`, `patientPaid`, and `tax` do not make R4 instances invalid in R6.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: These elements are not natively representable in R4 and should be profiled, extension-mapped, or dropped with documentation when producing R4 output.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds optional item-level subject
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `Claim.item.subject` is optional and therefore does not invalidate R4 Claim instances during forward migration.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: It can be important when the root subject is a group and a line item identifies an individual recipient. R4 has no direct item-level subject path.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds optional supportingInfo.subCategory
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element is optional and does not affect R4 instance validity in R6.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: R6-to-R4 conversion cannot preserve the finer-grained category natively unless extensions or category-code folding rules are used.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Required status and use code systems appear unchanged locally
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The versioned value-set references changed, but local CodeSystem concepts for `fm-status` and `claim-use` have the same code lists and definitions in the inspected packages.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology services may still return version-specific metadata, but no code-level break was identified for these required bindings from local package files.
